home.sharesAreBoughtAnd: Shares are bought and sold through a stock exchange, and exchanges keep office hours. When New York closes there is nobody on the other side of an order, so the price simply stops until it opens again. Crypto has no central exchange, which is why it never stops.
home.anIndexIsJust: An index is just a number calculated from the shares inside it. When the exchange those shares trade on is shut, there are no new prices to calculate it from, so the index sits still.
home.goldAndSilverAre: Gold and silver are priced on futures exchanges that close overnight and at weekends, the same way share exchanges do.
home.currenciesAreTradedBetween: Currencies are traded between banks rather than on one exchange, so the market runs around the clock from Sunday evening to Friday evening and then stops for the weekend while those desks are shut.

mpcharts.cxGuideSee: A flag only on a move we can explain with confidence - a story several desks carried, a liquidation cascade our feed measured, or a Bitcoin move with a known cause; a plain correction gets no flag. On the candle it started on, with the cause in one word: CPI, FOMC, a Bybit delisting, a hack, an ETF headline, a liquidation cascade - or a grey question mark where nothing dated explains it. A lime LIVE flag appears on the newest candle while a move is forming now.
mpcharts.cxGuideMeans: A move is measured against this coin’s own 30-day volatility, never a fixed percent. The cause comes from our Catalyst Engine: dated announcements, filings and fast news desks, matched to the move by symbol and by time (the news has to come inside 90 minutes BEFORE the move, or at most 30 minutes after, in which case the card says the market led the news). A cascade is our own feed liquidating six times the typical amount while the move ran. The month-wide line says how many moves were explained - that share is the honest measure of how much of this coin’s action is news-driven.
mpcharts.cxGuideL: A rise flagged with a dated catalyst is a move with a reason, and the question is whether the reason is still true; a rise flagged ? is flow, and flow reverses. Before a long, look at how the last three flagged rises resolved.
mpcharts.cxGuideS: A drop flagged Cascade is forced selling, which exhausts itself; a drop flagged with news (a delisting, a hack, a regulation headline) tends to keep its ground. Short the second kind, not the first.
mpcharts.circlesOnTheChart: Circles on the chart at the exact price and candle where a big liquidation happened in the last 24 hours. Red = a long was force-SOLD there, green = a short was force-BOUGHT. The bigger the circle, the bigger the position. Tap one for its size, the venue and how far it is from the price now.
mpcharts.theseAreNotForecasts: These are not forecasts and not a model - they are events our own collector recorded across eight exchanges. Where they cluster is where leverage actually died, and that price tends to matter again: it is where stops sat, and it is where the market proved somebody was offside. A wall of red circles under a drop is the cascade that caused it.
mpcharts.priceComingBackDown: Price coming back DOWN into a thick band of red circles is arriving where forced selling already happened once - either it gets absorbed and that is your level, or it breaks and the same thing happens again. Green circles above you mark where shorts were squeezed out; a move back up through them has fuel behind it.
mpcharts.theMirrorShortingInto: The mirror. Shorting into a band of green circles means shorting where short positions were already force-closed once. The emptier the chart, the calmer the market has been - which is information too.
mpcharts.oneLineBetween0: One line between 0 and 100. The shaded areas are above 70 and below 30.

mpcharts.aTurnUpOut: A turn up out of the oversold area, or a pullback that holds above 40 in an uptrend. Buying at 75 is buying the stretch.
mpcharts.aTurnDownOut: A turn down out of the overbought area, or a bounce that fails under 60 in a downtrend. Shorting at 25 is shorting the washout.

mpcharts.momentumTheMacdLine: Momentum. The MACD line crossing above the signal line is momentum turning up; the histogram shrinking while price still rises is momentum fading before price shows it.
mpcharts.aBullCrossFrom: A bull cross from below zero is the strongest form; a cross far above zero is late. Rising bars confirm, shrinking bars warn.
mpcharts.aBearCrossFrom: A bear cross from above zero. A histogram that peaks and shrinks while price makes a higher high is the classic exhaustion.

mpcharts.aDropOutOf: A drop out of the upper area. Pinned at -10 in a strong trend is strength, not a short.
mpcharts.oneLineAroundZero: One line around zero. Shaded past +100 and -100.

mpcharts.participationAMoveOn: Participation. A move on 2x average volume has people behind it; a breakout on half the average usually comes back.
mpcharts.aBreakoutCandleAt: A breakout candle at 1.5x or more, and a pullback that goes quiet. Rising price on falling volume is a move running out of buyers.
mpcharts.aBreakdownOnVolume: A breakdown on volume, a bounce on none. A selling climax (3x and more, long wick) often ends the fall rather than starts it.

mpcharts.theMirrorAStrong: The mirror. A strong bearish lean with fragility among the drivers is where cascades start.

mpcharts.aPoolBelowIs: A pool below is the target. A pool above is the squeeze risk - keep the stop beyond it.

mpheatmap.theRunningTotalAs: The running total as you walk away from the price. The row three ticks down does not show what sits at that price alone - it shows everything between the current price and there, so it answers "how much would I have to eat through to get that far".
mpheatmap.theThinColouredLine: The thin coloured line under each row, split by exchange. One colour means a single venue is holding that price on its own; four colours mean four books agree. A wall nobody else supports can disappear between two blinks.
mpheatmap.everyTradeHasA: Every trade has a patient side and an impatient one. mpheatmap.aLargeOrderEats: A large order eats the best price first, then the next, then the next - so the average price it actually gets is worse than the one on screen. This is that difference, measured by walking our real book, not estimated.
mpheatmap.aggressiveBuyingMinusAggre: Aggressive buying minus aggressive selling, in dollars, over the last few minutes. Positive means buyers were the impatient ones. Read it against the price: price grinding up while sellers are the aggressors means somebody is quietly absorbing them.
mpheatmap.aTradeFarLarger: A trade far larger than the rest of what is on screen - eight times the middle-sized print. Size alone does not predict anything, but a cluster of them on one side, at one price, is the market telling you where somebody with real money is working.
mpheatmap.howWideEachRow: How wide each row of the book is in price. Five exchanges quote to a fraction of a cent, so their prices are grouped into rows of this size - otherwise the ladder would be forty rows of dust instead of eight rows of size.
mpheatmap.exchangesDoNotTrade: Exchanges do not trade at exactly the same price - measured on Bitcoin, one venue sat $73 above the other four. mpheatmap.aPriceWhereA: A price where a crowd of leveraged positions would be force-closed. It is a MODEL, not a record: the exchange never publishes who is leveraged where, so this is estimated from price history. mpheatmap.howToReadIt: >HOW TO READ ITBright bands are crowds of traders whose long/short liquidation prices stack there — price tends to sweep the brightest ones, and a band disappears the moment price trades through it. On the map itself: a dot is a liquidation that really happened, a diamond is a level price has already swept, and a bar is an estimated liquidation level.
mpheatmap.footNumbers: WHAT THE NUMBERS MEANTap any level for two numbers that mean different things. What really liquidated is what our collector recorded actually being liquidated in that price band over the window you have picked - observed events, no estimate. The x typical figure is our estimate: how heavy that level is against a typical one on the same screen. It is a multiple and not a dollar amount on purpose - exchanges do not publish open positions, so every liquidation map reconstructs the crowd from price history and an assumed leverage mix (ours: 2x to 100x, weighted to 10-25x). That shows where size stacks relative to itself, not how many dollars sit in it. We tried scaling it by open interest and checked the result against reality: it overstated an average BTC level by roughly thirty times what has ever actually been liquidated in one, so it was dropped rather than shipped behind a disclaimer. Read a bright level as "there is probably size here", and trust the measured figure when the two disagree.
mpheatmap.footBook: READING THE ORDER BOOKThe order book is money that has not moved yet: red above the price is sellers waiting, green below is buyers. Size sits at that exact price, Sum adds it up as you walk away, and the bar behind each row is the total so far. The thin line under each row shows which exchanges hold that price — a wall one venue holds alone can vanish in a second, one that four venues share will not. The tape is money that just moved: an arrow up means the buyer crossed the spread and paid the offer, down means the seller hit the bid. Bright rows are prints far larger than the rest, and any print opens up on a click. Pick one exchange or All — and on All each book is lined up on its own mid first, because exchanges genuinely differ by a few dollars. None of this is modelled; the map above is.
mpheatmap.footData: DATAReal liquidations streamed live from Binance · Bybit · OKX · Hyperliquid (incl. stock & commodity perps) · Gate · HTX · dYdX · Bitfinex — eight venues, nine websocket feeds, and every figure above is what our collector actually received. We do not claim a share of the whole market, because nobody can measure one: no exchange publishes its own liquidation total, and Binance’s public liquidation stream sends at most one order per symbol per second, so on the venue that is the largest part of what we do see, our number is a floor rather than a total in exactly the minute a cascade makes it interesting. The bands are the one estimate on this page - our own model, from live price action, with entries laddered 2× to 100× and weighted to 10–25×.
